documentation.range: The Megamouth Shark is wide-ranging in tropical and temperate areas of all major oceans, although its full distribution remains poorly-known (Ebert et al. 2013, Haight 2018). Considerably more specimens are known from Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines in the Northwest and Western Central Pacific than elsewhere (Haight 2018).
documentation.population: The Megamouth Shark is a rare species; as of December 2018, it is known from 124 documented records (Haight 2018).
documentation.habitats: The Megamouth Shark occurs over the continental shelf and in oceanic waters; it has been recorded as shallow as 5 m depth in coastal waters, 40 m on the continental shelf, and offshore in the pelagic zone at 8–1,500 m depth in water 348–4,600 m deep (Yano et al. 1997, Ebert et al. 2013). The maximum reported size is ~800–900 cm total length (TL) (Martínez-Ortiz et al. 2017). The smallest known specimen was 177 cm TL, but it is unknown if this is close to the size at birth. The mode of reproduction is probably lecithotrophic viviparous with uterine cannibalism or oophagy (Ebert et al. 2013). The Megamouth Shark appears to be a vertical migrator, presumably following the vertical migrations of euphausiid prey (krill) during diel cycles (Compagno 2001).
documentation.threats: The Megamouth Shark is taken as rare, incidental bycatch of various high-seas and coastal fisheries, including commercial drift gillnets, set fish traps, and pelagic longlines, purse-seines, and trawls. Many early specimens have been utilized by museums and oceanaria for research and display, but the increasing number of captures from the Northwest and Western Central Pacific are highlighting potential increased interactions with fisheries. The Megamouth Shark is a bycatch of the driftnet fishery targeting Sharptail Mola (Masturus lanceolatus) over deep water off eastern Taiwan (Hsu et al. 2015). Sharptail Mola catches increased abruptly from 2000 (Liu et al. 2009), with 34 Megamouth Sharks recorded as bycatch in the fishery between April 2013 and May 2015 (Hsu et al. 2015). Dulvy et al. (2014) predicted, based on its body size and depth distribution, that the Megamouth Shark had a high likelihood of being threatened with an elevated risk of extinction if it was subjected to significant fisheries.
documentation.measures: Retention of the Megamouth Shark from United States Pacific fisheries has been prohibited since 2004. In 2015, the associated rule was refined to allow retention of incidentally caught Megamouth Sharks that are subsequently sold or donated for scientific, educational, research or display purposes. In Taiwan, it is mandatory to report Megamouth Shark catches to the government. Additional management of the Taiwanese sunfish driftnet fishery is recommended, including compulsory live release of incidentally caught Megamouth Sharks, and seasonal closure around the period of peak Megamouth Shark interactions (April to August). Globally, fisheries monitoring, including the collection of species-specific landings and discard data, is needed to support the development of population assessments and management advice. In the meantime, precautionary fishing limits and bycatch mitigation measures are warranted.
documentation.use_trade: This species has been consumed locally when caught in the Philippines, Taiwan, Brazil, and the Eastern Pacific (Martínez-Ortiz et al. 2017, Haight 2018).
documentation.rationale: The Megamouth Shark (Megachasma pelagios) is a large (to ~800-900 cm total length), pelagic filter-feeding shark distributed in oceanic habitats from approximately the surface down to 1,500 m in tropical waters worldwide. It is known from just over 120 documented specimens (as of December 2018), with considerably more records from Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines in the Northwest and Western Central Pacific than elsewhere. Outside of this area, it is rarely encountered. Recent levels of bycatch in the driftnet fishery targeting Sharptail Mola (Masturus lanceolatus) over deep water off eastern Taiwan raises some concern regarding the sustainability of catches. Further research on its ecology and habitat use are required to better understand this species and the potential effects of fishing. Based on its wide range, and generally limited interactions with fisheries, it is assessed as Least Concern. However, its increasing frequency of capture in Asia, particularly Taiwan, and its rarity and intrinsic sensitivity to overexploitation mean that captures in fisheries should be tracked carefully to ensure this species does not become threatened in the near future.
